title: Assessing the performance of 8 AI chatbots in bibliographic reference retrieval: Grok and DeepSeek outperform ChatGPT, but none are fully accurate
extended_summary:
This preprint examines how accurately eight free-access generative AI chatbots—ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok, Le Chat, and Perplexity—generate academic bibliographic references. The problem addressed is whether students can rely on general-purpose chatbots to retrieve legitimate, correctly formatted references for university academic work, given widespread concerns about hallucinated citations and inaccuracies in AI outputs.

The authors conducted a comparative evaluation using a standardized prompt asking each chatbot to provide 10 APA-formatted references in each of five university disciplines: cardiology, mechanical engineering, organic chemistry, sociology, and art history. Across the eight chatbots, this produced 400 references total. Each reference was manually checked against Google and Google Scholar for five elements: author, year, title, source, and locating data. The study also analyzed document type, age of references, error counts, citation counts, and overlap across chatbot outputs.

The study context is higher education and is framed around realistic student use of free chatbot versions for coursework or degree projects. No K-12 learners, classroom reading instruction, or school-supported foundational literacy intervention is studied. The population is implicitly university students as intended end users, not intervention participants receiving instruction. The work is therefore adjacent to educational technology use in higher education rather than evidence on learning outcomes.

The main conclusion is that these chatbots are not reliable for unverified bibliographic retrieval. Only 26.5% of generated references were fully correct, 33.8% were partially correct, and 39.8% were wrong or fabricated. Grok and DeepSeek performed best and did not fabricate references in this sample, but neither was fully accurate overall. The paper argues that universities should strengthen AI literacy and information literacy training so students verify AI-generated references rather than trusting them uncritically.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a higher-education preprint, not peer reviewed, and it is not a causal study of student outcomes. Although it has a clear descriptive methodology, it does not meet the K-12 causal evidence standard relevant to classroom effects on reading outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows practically important but non-causal evidence that chatbot use for academic reference retrieval has mixed utility and substantial risk. It does not estimate effects on K-12 learners or foundational reading outcomes, so educational impact is unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Comparative evaluation of eight general-purpose generative AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude) used by university students to generate academic bibliographic references in APA style across disciplinary domains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates the practical performance of 8 AI chatbots for bibliographic reference retrieval/generation rather than learning outcomes. Across 400 generated references, only 26.5% were fully correct, 33.8% partially correct, and 39.8% wrong or fabricated; Grok (60% fully correct) and DeepSeek (48%) outperformed others, while Copilot fabricated 100% of requested references. This suggests possible productivity benefits for sourcing references, but with severe reliability limitations that undermine dependable academic use.
finding.measure: Accuracy and reliability of generated bibliographic references (fully correct, partially correct, fabricated), mean errors per reference, overlap among chatbot outputs

finding.finding_summary: The study does not directly measure student critical thinking, but its empirical results imply risks for information-evaluation skills because 39.8% of references were wrong or fabricated and many outputs appeared plausible. The authors argue that uncritical reliance on chatbot outputs may impair verification and critical information use, especially among students who do not check sources manually.
finding.measure: Indirect institutional/behavioral implication drawn from hallucination and reference-accuracy analysis; no direct learner assessment
